text:
LONDON — Education Secretary Lucy Powell will travel to Beijing this week to promote closer ties between schools and universities in the two countries, as the U.K. government makes a fresh push for high-level engagement with China.
She will take part in a U.K.-China summit — the first for nine years — aimed at helping British educational institutions and businesses build new links with Beijing.
The trip is expected to expand opportunities for British providers of vocational training, overseas campuses, online learning and the export of educational materials such as textbooks, learning platforms and classroom supplies.
Powell’s visit comes days after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting hosted his Chinese counterpart, Dong Jun, in London. Streeting praised Andy Burnham’s government for having “stepped up our interaction with China.”
Powell said ahead of the summit that education was one of Britain’s “greatest strengths” and “expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.”
She vowed to use it to “support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”
Closer cooperation on education will form part of “clear-eyed engagement with China” by the government, she said, as she promised to champion freedom of speech and academic freedom during her trip.
Her efforts to promote British education abroad come despite the security services warning about the scale of Chinese attempts to spy on the U.K.
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China’s espionage operations by taking funding from a Chinese spy agency, MI5, the U.K.’s domestic intelligence agency, revealed in September .
Powell specified that she would seek to “protect U.K. institutions from any collaborations that could undermine national security, or attempts to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with U.K. universities.”
U.K. officials said the trip would recognize the contribution of the 150,000 Chinese students currently studying at U.K. universities rather than actively seeking to invite more.
